title: Chapter VI
paragraphs: Mr. Hindley returned for the funeral, bringing a wife—a surprise that astonished us and set the whole neighbourhood gossiping. He never told us who she was or where she came from. She probably had neither money nor family standing to recommend her, or he would hardly have hidden the marriage from his father.

Left to herself, she would not have caused much disturbance in the household. From the moment she crossed the threshold, everything she saw and everything happening around her seemed to delight her, except the preparations for the burial and the mourners' presence. Her behaviour then made me think she was half foolish. She rushed to her room and made me accompany her, though I ought to have been dressing the children. There she sat shaking and wringing her hands, asking over and over, “Have they gone yet?” Then she began describing hysterically how the sight of black clothes affected her, starting and trembling until she burst into tears. When I asked what was wrong, she said she did not know: she was simply so afraid of dying! I thought her no more likely to die than myself. She was rather thin, but young and fresh-faced, with eyes sparkling like diamonds. Admittedly, I noticed that climbing the stairs made her breathe rapidly, that any sudden noise sent her trembling, and that she sometimes had a troublesome cough. But I knew nothing of what such signs foretold and felt no urge to sympathise. We generally don't take to outsiders here, Mr. Lockwood, unless they take to us first.

Young Earnshaw had changed a good deal during his three years away. He was thinner and paler and spoke and dressed quite differently. The very day he returned he told Joseph and me that from then on we must keep to the back kitchen and leave the sitting room to him. In fact, he would have had a small spare room papered and carpeted to make a parlour; but his wife was so pleased with the white floor and enormous glowing fireplace, the pewter dishes, the dresser of crockery, the dog kennel and the space for moving about in their usual room that he decided she did not need the change for her comfort and abandoned it.

She was delighted, too, to discover a sister among her new acquaintances. At first she chatted to Catherine, kissed her, ran about with her and showered her with presents. Her affection soon wore out, however, and when she became irritable, Hindley became tyrannical. A few words from her expressing a dislike of Heathcliff awakened all his old hatred of the boy. He expelled him from their company to live with the servants, stopped his lessons with the curate, and ordered him to work outside instead, making him labour as hard as any other boy on the farm.

At first Heathcliff endured his lowered position fairly well, because Cathy passed on her lessons to him and worked or played beside him in the fields. Both seemed likely to grow up as uncivilised as savages. The young master cared nothing about their behaviour or activities so long as they stayed out of his way. He would not even have bothered about their attendance at church on Sundays if Joseph and the curate had not reproached him for neglect whenever they were absent. That reminded him to order a beating for Heathcliff and the loss of dinner or supper for Catherine. But one of their favourite pleasures was to escape onto the moors in the morning and stay out all day; the punishment afterwards became something merely to laugh at. The curate could give Catherine as many chapters to learn by heart as he liked, and Joseph could thrash Heathcliff until his arm ached: they forgot it all the moment they were together again, or at least once they had thought of some naughty revenge. Many times I cried privately to see them become more reckless every day, while I dared not speak for fear of losing the little influence I still had over those friendless creatures. One Sunday evening they happened to be sent out of the sitting room for making a noise or some equally small offence. When I called them for supper, they were nowhere to be found. We searched upstairs and down, the yard and the stables, but there was no sign of them. At last Hindley angrily ordered the doors bolted and swore that nobody should let them in that night. The household went to bed. Too anxious to lie down, I opened my window and leaned out to listen, despite the rain, determined to let them in if they returned, whatever the prohibition. After a while I heard footsteps on the road, and a lantern shone through the gate. I threw a shawl over my head and ran down before their knocking could wake Mr. Earnshaw. Heathcliff stood there alone. The sight of him by himself startled me.

“Where's Miss Catherine?” I asked quickly. “There hasn't been an accident, I hope?” “At Thrushcross Grange,” he answered, “and I'd have stayed there too, if they'd had the manners to invite me.” “Well, you're in for it!” I said. “You won't be satisfied until you're turned out. Whatever made you wander to Thrushcross Grange?” “Let me take off these wet clothes, and I'll explain, Nelly,” he replied. I warned him against waking the master. As he undressed, while I waited to put out the candle, he continued: “Cathy and I slipped out of the washhouse for a free ramble, and when we glimpsed the lights at the Grange we thought we'd go and see whether the Lintons spent Sunday evenings shivering in corners while their father and mother ate and drank, sang and laughed, and scorched their eyes in front of the fire. Do you suppose they do? Or read sermons and answer religious questions from their manservant, with a column of names from Scripture to learn if they get the answers wrong?” “Probably not,” I replied. “They're good children, no doubt, and don't deserve the punishment you earn by misbehaving.” “Don't be pious, Nelly,” he said. “Nonsense! We ran all the way from the Heights to the park without stopping. I beat Catherine easily because she had no shoes on. You'll have to look for them in the bog tomorrow. We crept through a broken hedge, felt our way along the path and settled in a flower bed beneath the drawing-room window. That was where the light came from: the shutters weren't up, and the curtains were only half drawn. Standing on the base of the wall and holding the ledge, we could both look inside. And what we saw—ah! It was beautiful: a magnificent room with a crimson carpet, crimson-covered chairs and tables, and a pure white ceiling edged in gold. A shower of glass drops hung on silver chains from its centre, gleaming with little gentle candles. Old Mr. and Mrs. Linton weren't there. Edgar and his sister had it all to themselves. Shouldn't they have been happy? We'd have thought ourselves in heaven! Now guess what your good children were doing. Isabella—I think she's eleven, a year younger than Cathy—was lying screaming at the far end of the room, shrieking as if witches were sticking red-hot needles into her. Edgar stood silently weeping on the hearth. In the middle of the table was a little dog, shaking its paw and yelping; we gathered from their accusations against each other that they'd nearly pulled it in half. The idiots! That was their pleasure! Arguing over who should hold a lump of warm fur, then both crying because, after fighting for it, neither would take it. We laughed aloud at the pampered things—how we despised them! When would you find me wanting something Catherine wanted? Or find the two of us alone, amusing ourselves by yelling, sobbing and rolling on the floor at opposite ends of a room? I wouldn't trade my life here for Edgar Linton's at Thrushcross Grange for a thousand lives—not even for the right to throw Joseph off the highest gable and paint the front of the house with Hindley's blood!”
“Hush, hush!” I broke in. “You still haven't explained, Heathcliff, how Catherine came to stay behind.”

“I told you we laughed,” he said. “The Lintons heard us and shot towards the door together like arrows. Everything went quiet, then came a cry: ‘Oh, mamma, mamma! Oh, papa! Oh, mamma, come here. Oh, papa, oh!’ They actually howled something like that. We made horrible noises to frighten them more, then dropped off the ledge, because someone was pulling back the bolts and we thought we'd better run. I held Cathy's hand and was hurrying her along when suddenly she fell. ‘Run, Heathcliff, run!’ she whispered. ‘They've let the bulldog out, and he's got hold of me!’ The devil had caught her ankle, Nelly; I heard his dreadful snorting. She didn't scream—no! She'd have scorned to scream even if a mad cow had impaled her on its horns. I did, though: I shouted enough curses to destroy any fiend in Christendom, and I grabbed a stone, forced it between his jaws and tried with all my strength to shove it down his throat. At last a brute of a servant came with a lantern, shouting, ‘Hold tight, Skulker, hold tight!’ He changed his tune when he saw what Skulker had caught. They choked the dog off her, his great purple tongue dangling six inches out of his mouth, his hanging lips streaming bloody drool. The man picked Cathy up. She was sick, from pain rather than fright, I'm certain. He carried her inside and I followed, muttering curses and threats of revenge. ‘What have you caught, Robert?’ Linton called from the doorway. ‘Skulker's caught a little girl, sir,’ he replied, ‘and here's a lad,’ he added, grabbing at me, ‘who looks a thorough villain! Likely enough some robbers meant to put them through the window to open the doors for the gang once we were asleep, so they could murder us at leisure. Hold your tongue, you foul-mouthed thief! You'll hang for this. Mr. Linton, sir, keep your gun ready.’ ‘No, no, Robert,’ said the old fool. ‘The rogues knew I collected my rents yesterday: they thought they'd catch me neatly. Bring them in; I'll give them a reception. John, fasten the chain. Jenny, give Skulker water. To challenge a magistrate in his own stronghold, and on the Sabbath too! Where will their impudence end? Oh, my dear Mary, look here! Don't be afraid; it's only a boy. Yet villainy is so plain on his scowling face, wouldn't hanging him now be a kindness to the country, before his actions show his nature as clearly as his features?’ He dragged me under the chandelier. Mrs. Linton put on her spectacles and threw up her hands in horror. The cowardly children crept closer too, Isabella lisping, ‘Horrible creature! Shut him in the cellar, papa. He's just like that fortune-teller's son who stole my tame pheasant. Isn't he, Edgar?’

“While they inspected me, Cathy recovered. She heard that last remark and laughed. After staring curiously at her, Edgar Linton found enough sense to recognise her. They see us at church, you know, though we hardly ever meet anywhere else. ‘It's Miss Earnshaw!’ he whispered to his mother. ‘And look where Skulker bit her—look how her foot's bleeding!’
“‘Miss Earnshaw? Ridiculous!’ the lady cried. ‘Miss Earnshaw roaming the countryside with a gypsy! But, my dear, the child's wearing mourning—surely it is her—and she may be crippled for life!’

“‘What blameworthy neglect on her brother's part!’ exclaimed Mr. Linton, turning away from me to Catherine. ‘Shielders has told me’”—that was the curate, sir—“‘that he lets her grow up an absolute heathen. But who is this? Where did she find this companion? Aha! I declare it's that strange acquisition my late neighbour brought back from Liverpool—a little Lascar, or an American or Spanish castaway.’
“‘A wicked boy, whatever he is,’ the old lady remarked, ‘and quite unfit for a respectable house! Did you hear his language, Linton? I'm appalled that our children were exposed to it.’

“I began swearing again—don't be angry, Nelly—so they ordered Robert to remove me. I wouldn't leave without Cathy. He dragged me into the garden, thrust the lantern into my hand and promised that Mr. Earnshaw would hear about my behaviour. Then he ordered me off and locked the door. One corner of the curtains was still looped back, so I returned to my spying place: if Catherine wanted to come home and they refused to let her, I meant to smash their great windows into a million pieces. She was sitting quietly on the sofa. Mrs. Linton took off the dairymaid's grey cloak, which we'd borrowed for our expedition, shaking her head and, I suppose, scolding her. Cathy was a young lady, so they made a difference between her treatment and mine. A maid brought a bowl of warm water and washed her feet; Mr. Linton mixed a glass of warm spiced wine, Isabella tipped a plateful of cakes into her lap, and Edgar stood some distance away gaping. Then they dried and combed her lovely hair, put enormous slippers on her, and wheeled her to the fire. I left her as happy as could be, sharing her food between the little dog and Skulker, whose nose she pinched while he ate, and lighting a spark in the Lintons' empty blue eyes—a faint reflection of her own enchanting face. I could see they were full of foolish admiration. She's so far above them—above everyone in the world—isn't she, Nelly?”

“More will come of this than you expect,” I told him, covering him up and putting out the light. “There's no curing you, Heathcliff, and Mr. Hindley will have to take extreme measures. You see if he doesn't.” My words proved truer than I wanted. Earnshaw was furious at their unfortunate adventure. To improve matters further, Mr. Linton himself visited next day and lectured the young master so severely on his management of the family that he was stirred into taking a serious look around him. Heathcliff was not beaten, but was told that the first word he addressed to Miss Catherine would get him dismissed. Mrs. Earnshaw undertook to keep her sister-in-law properly in order when she returned, using cunning rather than force: by force she would never have managed it.
